A1.justification: Both complete, readable 25-page PDFs describe SPEAR. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison despite substantial rewriting and some internal reporting inconsistencies.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPEAR fine-tuning, SUPERB and HEAR results, together with teacher-selection, loss-weighting, codebook and representation analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds token-mixing, architecture, quantisation-target, teacher-layer and USAD comparison experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.3 introduces power-weighted stochastic token mixing, changing supervision for mixed waveforms to incorporate both sources' targets. MVQ, Zipformer and the main asymmetric objective remain. The revised asymmetry description also resolves v1's appendix/main-text contradiction rather than demonstrating a reversal of the underlying method.

E1.justification: The named main training corpora and evaluation tasks are retained, including SUPERB, HEAR and low-resource LibriSpeech tests. However, the new USAD-aligned experiment in Appendix G provides training totals and excluded corpora without listing the included corpora. Whether this introduces different training populations cannot be established from the PDFs.

E2.justification: v2 adds USAD Base/Large to ASR and audio-tagging fine-tuning comparisons and introduces Dasheng 1.2B in SUPERB, where ATST-Frame disappears. HuBERT Large and Dasheng-Base fine-tuning comparisons are removed. New denoising, Transformer and k-means controls further expand the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces token mixing on 10% of training samples with sampled SNRs between -5 and 5. New experimental protocols include 300k-update architecture/target comparisons, a 2000-cluster k-means control using masked-only loss, teacher-layer sweeps and a 95.3k-hour USAD-aligned training configuration. Existing benchmark metrics and principal fine-tuning splits remain.

E4.justification: New studies test token mixing against denoising, teacher-layer selection, Zipformer versus Transformer, MVQ versus k-means targets, dual-domain loss weighting and the influence of teacher choice in comparison with USAD. Existing teacher-model, codebook-count, masked-loss and UMAP analyses remain. The original dual-domain strategy study moves into Section 5.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; stochastic augmentation is not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous new control results and revised benchmark values appear. With revised pre-training, SPEARs Large reports diarisation error changing from 3.20 to 2.30 and separation SI-SDRi from 11.20 to 11.67 (v1 Table 13; v2 Table 14). Its dual-domain Large concatenated HEAR average changes from 81.78 to 82.46 in the main tables; v2 Table 16 retains 81.8 despite individual scores supporting approximately 82.46.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions of stochastic token selection, temporal offset and the signal-power mixing coefficient in Equations 4–5. Existing MVQ reconstruction, quantiser-training and masked-prediction mathematics remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof establishes the asserted teacher-performance bound.

C1.justification: v2 drops the repeated claim of being the first unified speech-and-audio SSL framework and makes complementary teacher distillation, domain fusion and token-mixing robustness central contributions. The broad unified-representation and SUPERB leadership claims remain, but the claimed contribution set changes substantially.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting secondary-source preservation to robustness, Dasheng's speech weaknesses to its MAE objective, and backbone choice to efficiency and fine-tuning performance. Appendix G newly argues that feature matching imposes teacher-performance limits and risks semantically inappropriate cross-domain averages. These are interpretations rather than proved guarantees. Existing data-imbalance and voice-conversion limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses NVIDIA A800 80GB hardware, GPU counts and approximate GPU hours in Table 9, plus token-mixing sampling and SNR details. Conversely, it omits v1's quantiser-training disclosures of 100 LibriSpeech hours and 50 balanced-AudioSet hours. Both versions still promise future code and model release.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around EncodecMAE, MT2KD and USAD, with expanded distinctions between discrete prediction and feature matching. A new discussion compares SPEAR with SALMONN, Audio Flamingo 3 and Qwen-omni. Earlier discussions and citations concerning MERT, SSAST and general model-compression distillation are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. v2 adds a main-text ablation section, reorganises the appendices, changes Ethics Statement to Impact Statement, and removes standalone Reproducibility Statement and LLM Usage sections. Terminology and section titles are also revised.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one-column to two-column layout. v2 adds a token-mixing diagram and multiple experimental tables, resizes existing displays, restructures HEAR tables by training-data scale, and changes the selected SUPERB columns. The original loss-sensitivity and UMAP plots are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices through architecture and same-teacher-layer target comparisons, teacher-matched USAD evaluation, and a direct token-mixing ablation. These address attribution gaps in v1's largely cross-model comparisons. Corrected asymmetric-loss documentation and compute disclosures also help assessment. Imperfect controls, unproved feature-matching claims, stale HEAR appendix averages and omitted quantiser-training details remain drawbacks, but the targeted experimental evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
